papers.title: SciSciGPT: advancing human–AI collaboration in the science of science
papers.abstract: We introduce SciSciGPT, an open-source, prototype artificial intelligence (AI) collaborator that uses the domain of science of science as a testbed to explore the potential of large language model-powered research tools. SciSciGPT automates complex workflows, supports diverse analytical approaches, accelerates research prototyping and iteration and facilitates reproducibility. Through case studies, we demonstrate its ability to streamline a wide range of empirical and analytical research tasks while highlighting its broader potential to advance research. We further propose a large language model agent capability maturity model for human–AI collaboration, envisioning a roadmap to further improve and expand upon frameworks such as SciSciGPT. As AI capabilities continue to evolve, frameworks such as SciSciGPT may play increasingly pivotal roles in scientific research and discovery. At the same time, these new advances also raise critical challenges, from ensuring transparency and ethical use to balancing human and AI contributions. Addressing these issues may shape the future of scientific inquiry and inform how we train the next generation of scientists to thrive in an increasingly AI-integrated research ecosystem.

papers.title: XtraGPT: Context-Aware and Controllable Academic Paper Revision via Human-AI Collaboration
papers.abstract: Despite the growing adoption of large language models (LLMs) in academic workflows, their capabilities remain limited in supporting high-quality scientific writing. Most existing systems are designed for general-purpose scientific text generation and fail to meet the sophisticated demands of research communication beyond surface-level polishing, for example, maintaining conceptual coherence across sections. Furthermore, academic writing is inherently iterative and revision-driven, a process that is not well supported by direct prompting-based paradigms. To address these scenarios, we propose a human-AI collaboration framework for academic paper revision, centered on criteria-guided intent alignment and context-aware modeling. To validate the framework, we curate a dataset of 7,000 research papers from top-tier venues, annotated with 140,000 instruction--response pairs that reflect realistic, section-level scientific revisions. We instantiate the framework in XtraGPT, the first suite of open-source LLMs (1.5B to 14B parameters) specifically fine-tuned for context-aware academic paper revision. Extensive experiments show that XtraGPT significantly outperforms same-scale baselines and rivals the quality of proprietary counterparts. Both automated preference assessments and human evaluations confirm the effectiveness of XtraGPT in improving scientific drafts. Our code and models are available at https://github.com/Xtra-Computing/XtraGPT and https://huggingface.co/collections/Xtra-Computing/xtragpt.

papers.title: DeBiasMe: De-biasing Human-AI Interactions with Metacognitive AIED (AI in Education) Interventions
papers.abstract: While generative artificial intelligence (Gen AI) increasingly transforms academic environments, a critical gap exists in understanding and mitigating human biases in AI interactions, such as anchoring and confirmation bias. This position paper advocates for metacognitive AI literacy interventions to help university students critically engage with AI and address biases across the Human-AI interaction workflows. The paper presents the importance of considering (1) metacognitive support with deliberate friction focusing on human bias; (2) bi-directional Human-AI interaction intervention addressing both input formulation and output interpretation; and (3) adaptive scaffolding that responds to diverse user engagement patterns. These frameworks are illustrated through ongoing work on "DeBiasMe," AIED (AI in Education) interventions designed to enhance awareness of cognitive biases while empowering user agency in AI interactions. The paper invites multiple stakeholders to engage in discussions on design and evaluation methods for scaffolding mechanisms, bias visualization, and analysis frameworks. This position contributes to the emerging field of AI-augmented learning by emphasizing the critical role of metacognition in helping students navigate the complex interaction between human, statistical, and systemic biases in AI use while highlighting how cognitive adaptation to AI systems must be explicitly integrated into comprehensive AI literacy frameworks.

papers.title: Designing AI Systems that Augment Human Performed vs. Demonstrated Critical Thinking
papers.abstract: The recent rapid advancement of LLM-based AI systems has accelerated our search and production of information. While the advantages brought by these systems seemingly improve the performance or efficiency of human activities, they do not necessarily enhance human capabilities. Recent research has started to examine the impact of generative AI on individuals' cognitive abilities, especially critical thinking. Based on definitions of critical thinking across psychology and education, this position paper proposes the distinction between demonstrated and performed critical thinking in the era of generative AI and discusses the implication of this distinction in research and development of AI systems that aim to augment human critical thinking.

summary: The literature on Human-AI collaboration in scientific research proposal generation reveals two primary themes: the enhancement of scientific discovery through AI augmentation and the integration of AI tools in academic workflows. While advancements like SciSciGPT and XtraGPT demonstrate potential in automating research processes and improving writing quality, challenges such as ethical concerns, transparency, and cognitive biases remain significant. Gaps in empirical validation and the need for comprehensive frameworks to balance human and AI contributions highlight areas for further exploration and development.
literature_tension_graph: The literature presents a tension between the effectiveness of AI tools like SciSciGPT and XtraGPT in automating research processes and the ethical implications surrounding their use, particularly regarding transparency and bias (mechanism conflict). While SciSciGPT claims to streamline workflows, it raises concerns about the balance of human and AI contributions, which remains unresolved. Additionally, the literature suggests that existing AI systems may not genuinely enhance critical thinking, despite claims of improved efficiency (evaluation conflict). This discrepancy highlights a gap in empirical validation of AI's impact on cognitive engagement in research. Future research should explore frameworks that not only enhance AI capabilities but also critically assess their ethical implications and cognitive effects, aiming to reconcile these conflicting claims.
scholarly_positioning: Previous research on Human-AI collaboration in scientific proposal generation has primarily focused on the automation of workflows and enhancement of writing quality through tools like SciSciGPT and XtraGPT. However, these approaches often overlook the ethical implications and the need for frameworks that effectively balance human and AI contributions, leading to unresolved tensions in transparency and cognitive biases. The existing literature lacks comprehensive empirical validation and a nuanced understanding of how these collaborations can genuinely augment critical thinking and research outcomes. This proposed research aims to address these gaps by developing a robust framework that not only enhances AI capabilities but also empowers researchers to navigate biases and improve cognitive engagement, thereby contributing to a more effective and ethically sound integration of AI in scientific research.
research_scope: This study will investigate the effectiveness of the SciSciGPT AI system in enhancing the proposal generation process among academic researchers in the fields of social sciences and humanities. The evaluation period will span six months, during which researchers will utilize SciSciGPT for generating research proposals, compared to a control group using traditional methods. Primary outcomes will include writing quality assessments based on peer reviews and user satisfaction scores, while secondary outcomes will measure cognitive engagement and the prevalence of cognitive biases through pre- and post-intervention surveys. The study aims to develop a framework that integrates metacognitive interventions to enhance user capabilities and address biases in Human-AI collaboration.
concept_definition:
{
  "Human-AI Collaboration": "The interaction between human researchers and AI systems, specifically in the context of generating research proposals, where AI assists in the ideation and drafting process.",
  "User Trust": "The degree to which researchers believe in the reliability and competence of the AI system, operationalized through metrics like trust calibration (accuracy of user expectations) and perceived transparency (clarity of AI processes).",
  "Cognitive Engagement": "The level of mental involvement and critical thinking exhibited by researchers when using AI tools, measured through pre- and post-intervention surveys assessing engagement levels.",
  "Cognitive Biases": "Systematic patterns of deviation from norm or rationality in judgment that can affect decision-making, evaluated through specific measures in user surveys before and after AI tool usage.",
  "Writing Quality": "The standard of written proposals, assessed through peer reviews that evaluate clarity, coherence, and originality.",
  "Metacognitive Interventions": "Strategies designed to enhance researchers' awareness and regulation of their cognitive processes, aimed at mitigating biases and improving decision-making in collaboration with AI.",
  "Ethical AI Integration": "The incorporation of ethical considerations into AI systems, ensuring that their use does not compromise user autonomy or lead to harmful outcomes, evaluated through user feedback and ethical frameworks.",
  "AI System Performance Data": "Quantitative metrics that assess the effectiveness and efficiency of the AI tool (SciSciGPT) in generating proposals, including output quality and user satisfaction.",
  "Interpretability": "The degree to which the internal workings of the AI model can be understood by users, potentially using methods like attention visualization (showing which parts of input influence outputs) and explanation generation (providing rationales for AI decisions).",
  "Safety Outcomes": "Metrics that indicate the potential risks associated with AI usage, such as unsafe response rate (frequency of harmful outputs) and refusal precision/recall (accuracy of the AI in declining inappropriate requests)."
}

theoretical_mechanism: In this study, the independent variable is the use of the SciSciGPT AI system for research proposal generation. The dependent variables are writing quality and cognitive biases among academic researchers. The mediator for user-level outcomes is perceived transparency, which influences user trust and satisfaction. The moderator is the level of cognitive engagement, which may enhance or diminish the effects of AI assistance on writing quality and bias mitigation. The theoretical framework is grounded in Human-Computer Interaction (HCI) and cognitive psychology, positing that effective AI integration can enhance critical thinking through improved transparency and engagement. System-level outcomes, such as unsafe response rates, are mediated by technical mechanisms like safety filters and representation features. Assumptions requiring empirical validation include the effectiveness of metacognitive interventions in reducing cognitive biases and the reliability of AI-generated outputs in enhancing proposal quality.
hypothesis: The use of the SciSciGPT AI system for research proposal generation (independent variable) will lead to higher writing quality (primary dependent variable) compared to traditional methods (comparison/control), mediated by increased perceived transparency, resulting in enhanced user trust and satisfaction.

methodology: This study will employ a mixed-methods approach, utilizing a controlled experimental design with a within-subject comparison of research proposal generation using the SciSciGPT AI system versus traditional methods among academic researchers in the social sciences and humanities. Participants will be recruited and randomly assigned to either the AI-assisted group or the control group, with both groups generating proposals over a six-month period. Key operationalized variables include writing quality, assessed through peer reviews, and cognitive biases, measured via pre- and post-intervention surveys. Evaluation metrics will encompass user trust scores, cognitive engagement levels, and writing quality assessments. To control for confounding variables, participant demographics and prior experience with AI tools will be collected and analyzed. The study aims to ensure reproducibility by adhering to standardized protocols for proposal generation and evaluation metrics, while also addressing the ethical implications of AI integration through metacognitive interventions designed to enhance user capabilities.
